summary:
Legal gender recognition in Taiwan remains gated by a 2008 executive order requiring sex-reassignment surgery before a gender marker can be changed on the national ID. An estimated 90% of trans people are blocked from obtaining a document that matches their presentation, which turns every ID-requiring interaction, including clinic visits and airport security checks, into a potential site of distress and disclosure. The Ministry of Health and Welfare has recognised gender self-determination as a human right since 2013, but the surgical requirement stands.

On 19 August 2024 a Taipei court denied a transgender woman's request to change her ID marker without surgery or a psychological evaluation, and the rights group supporting her indicated that an appeal was likely. No later ruling on this question is documented in this record. During 2025 no tangible policy change occurred on abolishing the surgery requirement or on expanding assisted reproduction access.

Assisted reproduction is restricted by statute. The Artificial Reproduction Act limits IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies to legally married heterosexual couples, specifically excluding same-sex female couples and single women.

Facilities provision is expanding but uneven. The Ministry of Environment will invest NT$280 million over four years to double gender-neutral public bathrooms nationwide from 623 to 1,246 by 2029. Of trans and gender-neutral survey respondents who reported discrimination, 17% said the discrimination occurred in public restrooms or changing rooms. In November 2025 an LGBTQ+ rights group found that only 5 of 149 government-listed all-gender toilets met the required standards, including clear all-gender signage.

Statutory protection is substantial on paper. Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender characteristics has been banned in education nationwide since the Gender Equity Education Act of June 2004, which carries a fine of NT$100,000 for schools discriminating in admission, instruction or assessment. Employment discrimination based on sexual orientation has been prohibited since the 2007–08 amendments to the Employment Service Act and the Act of Gender Equality in Employment, with fines of NT$300,000 to NT$1,500,000. The Long-Term Care Services Act of January 2017 contains an anti-discrimination clause covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and Judicial Yuan Interpretation No. 748 of 24 May 2017 held that the Constitution's Article 7 grounds of discrimination are illustrative rather than exhaustive, so sexual orientation is protected by the right to equality.

Conversion therapy is effectively banned by a Ministry of Health and Welfare letter of 22 February 2018, with violators liable under the Criminal Code or the Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act.

Private, consensual same-sex sexual activity between adults is legal, and the age of consent is 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Anti-gender political activity is rising. Analysis published in November 2024 described a wave of anti-gender discourse, and reporting from January 2026 recorded organisations promoting a foreign government's anti-trans policies alongside a political party calling for a 'two genders' position, against a backdrop described as continued transphobia through 2025.

The 7th annual Taiwan Transgender March in Taipei drew an estimated 3,000 people in November 2025 despite rain, with international participants, and called for an end to discrimination against trans people as the rights debate continues.

In November 2018 voters passed a referendum question banning LGBT-inclusive sex education in schools and rejected the pro-inclusion question; the Education Minister said LGBT content would be reviewed against the result, and an earlier Ministry of Education curriculum reform announced in March 2010 and effective in 2011 had already been watered down to 'respecting diverse sexual orientations' after opposition. Suicide hotlines reported a 40% surge in calls from LGBT individuals, particularly adolescents and young adults, after that referendum.

Taiwan is routinely described as among the most liberal jurisdictions in its region for LGBT rights, and the first Taiwan Pride was held in Taipei on 1 November 2003 with over 1,000 attendees, growing to about 80,000 by 2015, 137,000 in 2018 and 170,000 by 2019, with pride events also held in Kaohsiung since 2010 and Taichung. In 2022 Taiwan withdrew from hosting WorldPride 2025 over the disputed event name, which the public and government considered offensive, and the event moved to Washington, D.C. in June 2025. That progressive reputation sits alongside the surgical gate on legal gender recognition and the court refusal of August 2024.
localsOnly:
Conscription criteria were under revision in 2025, and pending changes were reported as capable of actively harming trans people. Whether those changes were enacted is not sourced here.

Family law is resident-facing and has moved faster than gender recognition. Same-sex couples can legally adopt, and since May 2023 legislation has granted full adoption rights, replacing the partial stepchild-only adoption rights in place since 2019; a January 2022 court order had already allowed a same-sex couple to adopt before the legislature codified full rights. Taiwan law also permits single individuals, including individual LGBT people, to adopt depending on circumstances.

Education content remains constrained by the 2018 referendum result, with LGBT material subject to review against it, and the anti-discrimination duties of the Gender Equity Education Act, including the sexual-bullying prevention and reporting duties added in June 2011, continue to bind schools.

Community infrastructure exists across the country: listings of organisations, bars, spas and venues are maintained for 12 cities, and the country's LGBT organisations were described in a resources page as among the most developed in the region.
outOfScopeNotes:
A source page specifically addressing Taiwan's transgender rights laws, protections and gaps was unavailable at research time, returning HTTP 404 after removal; its content is not reflected here and the gaps it may have documented remain unresolved.

The 90% figure for trans people blocked from a matching national ID is presented by the source as an estimate; no methodology, survey population or reference year is given.

The 17% restroom and changing-room discrimination figure is reported without a survey period, so its currency cannot be established from the source.

The outcome of the appeal flagged after the August 2024 Taipei court refusal is not sourced, and no later decision on surgery-free marker change is documented.

The employment prohibitions are stated in the source as covering sexual orientation; whether gender identity is equally covered in employment, as it is in education and long-term care, is not resolved by this inventory.

Whether the pending conscription-criteria changes took effect, and on what terms, is not sourced.
